name: Sandro
line: The Brazilian enforcer N17 adopted as its own. Big energy, a bigger smile, and a story about starting again far from home.
bio: Sandro arrived from Internacional in 2010 and quickly became one of the Lane's favourite players: a ball-winner who played with his heart on his sleeve and celebrated every tackle as if it were a goal.
His Spurs years were also shaped by serious injury. Coming back from it, and later from a move away, gives him a grounded, funny and honest take on resilience, belonging and staying hungry.
He still pulls on the shirt for the Spurs former players team, and the crowd's reaction shows he never really left.
why: Best for audiences who want energy and warmth: kick-offs, client dinners and international teams adapting to a new environment.
timeline: Becomes a fixture in the Spurs midfield
Moves on after four seasons in N17
Turns out for the Spurs former players team and works with fans and partners

name: Dele Alli
honour: PFA Young Player of the Year ×2
line: From League One to a World Cup semi-final in three years. A candid voice on pressure, fame and what it takes to rebuild.
bio: Dele joined from MK Dons in 2015 and was an instant hit: inventive, fearless and decisive in big games. He was named PFA Young Player of the Year twice and became a central figure in the side that reached the 2019 Champions League final.
With England he played at the 2018 World Cup, where the team reached the semi-finals.
Since leaving Spurs he has spoken openly about mental health and the pressure that comes with early success. Those conversations land with audiences far beyond football.
why: Best for audiences who want honesty: wellbeing programmes, early-careers cohorts and leaders managing high-potential talent.
timeline: PFA Young Player of the Year

name: Mauricio Pochettino
honour: Led Spurs to the 2019 Champions League final
line: The coach who built a young, hungry Spurs side and took it to a Champions League final. A masterclass in culture and belief.
bio: Mauricio Pochettino arrived in 2014 and turned Spurs into one of Europe's most energetic, intense teams. He promoted young players, demanded relentless standards and built a squad with a deep sense of belonging.
His era brought regular Champions League football, a title challenge and the club's first Champions League final in 2019, reached after the unforgettable comeback in Amsterdam.
His later roles at the highest level of club and international football mean bookings are limited and planned well in advance.
why: Best for senior leadership audiences interested in culture, developing talent and leading through belief.
timeline: Leads a sustained Premier League title challenge
Champions League final after the semi-final comeback in Amsterdam

name: Harry Redknapp
honour: Took Spurs into the Champions League
line: Took over a side bottom of the table and led it into the Champions League. Football's great storyteller.
bio: Harry Redknapp took charge in autumn 2008 with Spurs at the foot of the table. Within two seasons the club had finished in the top four and reached the Champions League, going on to a quarter-final in its first campaign.
His man-management, built on trust, humour and getting the best out of big personalities, is the core of his talks.
He is one of football's best-loved storytellers, with a natural gift for a room and a lifetime of dressing-room stories.
why: Best for after-dinner audiences, client entertaining and any team that needs a turnaround story.
timeline: Appointed Spurs manager with the club bottom of the league
Top-four finish and Champions League qualification

name: Ledley King
line: Academy graduate, club captain and one-club man. Leadership and loyalty from someone who lived them.
bio: Ledley King came through the Spurs academy and spent his entire playing career at the club. He became one of the finest defenders of his generation and captained the side.
A chronic knee condition meant he often played without training between matches, a remarkable story of managing your body and your mindset to keep performing.
As captain he lifted the 2008 League Cup. Today he represents the club as an ambassador.
why: Best for audiences exploring leadership, loyalty and sustained performance under constraint.
timeline: Captains Spurs to the League Cup

name: Clive Allen
honour: From the pitch to the dugout
line: Scored a record 49 goals in one season, then went back to the training ground as a coach. From the pitch to the dugout.
bio: Clive Allen's 1986–87 season is one of the great individual campaigns in Spurs history: 49 goals in all competitions and both major Player of the Year awards.
He later returned to the club as a coach, working with the first team and briefly stepping in as caretaker, so he sees the game from both sides of the touchline.
That pairing of elite finishing and coaching experience makes him a strong speaker on focus, marginal gains and helping others perform.
why: Best for audiences who want two angles on performance: the player who delivered and the coach who develops.
timeline: 49 goals in a season; Player of the Year
Returns as a coach, including a spell as caretaker

name: Glenn Hoddle
line: The Lane's great artist, who came back to manage the club he grew up at. Vision, craft and seeing the game from both sides of the touchline.
bio: Glenn Hoddle came through the Spurs youth system and became one of the most gifted English midfielders of his generation: a passer and goalscorer who could change a game with one touch. He won the FA Cup with Spurs in 1981 and again in 1982, scoring in the 1982 final and its replay.
He left for Monaco in 1987, winning the French title under Arsène Wenger, before moving into management with Swindon Town and Chelsea, then taking charge of England at the 1998 World Cup.

In 2001 he returned to White Hart Lane as manager and led Spurs to the 2002 League Cup final. Today he is a respected broadcaster, and his story of talent, leadership and recovering from a cardiac arrest in 2018 resonates well beyond football.
why: Best for audiences interested in creativity, leadership and the jump from star performer to manager.
timeline: First-team debut after coming through the youth ranks
Leads Spurs to the League Cup final

name: Pat Jennings
pos: Goalkeeper 1964–1977 · later goalkeeping coach · Northern Ireland
line: One of the greatest goalkeepers the game has seen, who later spent years passing on his craft to the next generation of Spurs keepers.
bio: Pat Jennings joined Spurs from Watford in 1964 and became one of the finest goalkeepers in world football, famous for his huge hands, calm authority and a habit of making the impossible look simple.

His Spurs years brought the 1967 FA Cup, two League Cups and the 1972 UEFA Cup, and he was named Football Writers' Footballer of the Year in 1973. Internationally he was a fixture for Northern Ireland, playing at the 1982 and 1986 World Cups.
After retiring he returned to Spurs as a goalkeeping coach, working with young keepers for many years. That makes him a rare voice on both sides of mastery: performing at the top, then teaching it.
why: Best for audiences who value calm under pressure, longevity and mentoring the next generation.
timeline: Returns to Spurs as a goalkeeping coach

name: Jermain Defoe
honour: Five goals in one Premier League game
line: A natural finisher who came back for a second spell and never stopped scoring. Sharp on preparation, self-belief and giving back.
bio: Jermain Defoe joined Spurs from West Ham in 2004 and quickly showed why he was one of the sharpest finishers in the country. After a short spell at Portsmouth he returned in 2009, and later that year scored five times in a 9–1 win over Wigan Athletic.
He was part of the Redknapp side that reached the Champions League, and with England he played at the 2010 World Cup. His career later took him to Toronto, Sunderland, Bournemouth and Rangers.
He talks with real warmth about preparation, confidence and using a platform for good.
why: Best for sales and performance audiences who want energy, a finisher's mindset and a story about purpose.
timeline: Joins Tottenham Hotspur from West Ham
Returns to Spurs; scores five against Wigan
Plays at the World Cup with England

name: Gary Mabbutt
honour: Captain of the 1991 FA Cup winners
line: Sixteen years at Spurs, a UEFA Cup and an FA Cup lifted as captain, all while managing type 1 diabetes. Leadership without excuses.
bio: Gary Mabbutt joined from Bristol Rovers in 1982 and stayed for sixteen seasons, playing across defence and midfield with the same commitment wherever he was asked to play. He was part of the side that won the UEFA Cup in 1984.
As captain he climbed the Wembley steps to lift the FA Cup in 1991. He did all of this while living with type 1 diabetes, and became a prominent advocate for people managing the condition.

Appointed MBE for his services to football, he remains closely connected to the club. His talks combine captaincy, consistency and an honest account of performing at the top while managing a lifelong health condition.
why: Best for leadership and wellbeing audiences who want a story about consistency, resilience and leading by example.
timeline: Joins Tottenham Hotspur from Bristol Rovers
Plays in the FA Cup final
Lifts the FA Cup as captain
Retires after sixteen seasons at Spurs

name: Jan Vertonghen
line: The calm, ball-playing centre-back at the heart of Pochettino's Spurs. A thoughtful voice on partnerships, consistency and coming back from setbacks.
bio: Jan Vertonghen arrived from Ajax in 2012 and became one of the most dependable defenders in the Premier League: composed on the ball, smart without it and a leader in the back line.

His partnership with fellow Belgian Toby Alderweireld underpinned the Pochettino era, including the 2019 run to the Champions League final. With Belgium he helped the national side finish third at the 2018 World Cup and became the country's most-capped men's player.
After leaving Spurs in 2020 he played for Benfica and Anderlecht. He speaks thoughtfully about trust between team-mates, long-term consistency and returning from injury.
why: Best for audiences exploring partnership, trust and quiet, consistent leadership.
timeline: Third place at the World Cup with Belgium

name: Bethany England
honour: Captained Spurs in the 2024 FA Cup final
line: The England striker who led Spurs Women's attack and wore the armband on their first Women's FA Cup final day. Drive, standards and backing yourself.
bio: Bethany England joined Tottenham Hotspur Women from Chelsea in January 2023 and immediately gave the side a cutting edge, scoring regularly and bringing a winning mentality from her years at the top of the WSL.
In 2024 she helped Spurs reach the Women's FA Cup final for the first time, wearing the captain's armband at Wembley. She has represented England at senior level.
Her story of moving to a club with big ambitions and taking responsibility for driving them on makes her a strong voice on leadership, high standards and the growth of the women's game.
why: Best for audiences who want energy and ambition: women's networks, sales teams and brands investing in the women's game.
timeline: Joins Tottenham Hotspur Women from Chelsea
Captains Spurs in the Women's FA Cup final at Wembley
Professional footballer and advocate for the women's game

name: Gareth Bale
honour: PFA Players' Player of the Year ×2
line: The teenage left-back who became the best player in the league in a Spurs shirt. A story about patience, reinvention and handling the biggest stage.
bio: Gareth Bale joined Spurs from Southampton in 2007 as a teenage left-back, and his early months in N17 were far from easy. Moved further forward, he was transformed, and a second-half hat-trick at San Siro against Inter in 2010 announced him to the whole of Europe.

By 2013 he was the most feared attacker in the Premier League, collecting the PFA and FWA awards before a world-record move to Real Madrid, where he won the Champions League five times. He came back to Spurs on loan for the 2020–21 season, and the welcome said everything about how fans remember him.

With Wales he became the national team's record goalscorer and led a golden generation to a European Championship semi-final and a first World Cup in decades. Since retiring in 2023 he has become a calm, thoughtful presence on Champions League broadcasts.
why: Best for audiences who want a world-class performer on reinvention: leadership offsites, flagship client events and brand moments that need a global name.
timeline: Hat-trick against Inter at San Siro
Wins the PFA and FWA awards; moves to Real Madrid
Returns to Spurs on a season-long loan

name: Robbie Keane
pos: Striker · Tottenham Hotspur 2002–2011 · Republic of Ireland
line: Cartwheel celebrations, a Wembley trophy and a goalscoring record for his country. Now a manager with a winner’s view on building teams.
bio: Robbie Keane arrived from Leeds United in 2002 and became the heartbeat of the Spurs attack, famous for his work rate, his finishing and the cartwheel celebration that every young fan copied in the playground.

He was part of the side that beat Chelsea at Wembley to win the 2008 League Cup, the club's first major trophy in nearly a decade. After a brief move to Liverpool he returned to N17, and later won three MLS Cups with LA Galaxy. For the Republic of Ireland he is the record goalscorer and the most-capped men's player.
He has since moved into coaching and management, including a league title with Maccabi Tel Aviv, and is a regular for the Spurs former players team at the stadium.
why: Best for sales and leadership audiences who want a born competitor on winning habits, coming back stronger and building a team culture.
timeline: Joins Tottenham Hotspur from Leeds United
Wins the League Cup at Wembley
Returns to Spurs after a spell at Liverpool
Joins LA Galaxy; goes on to win three MLS Cups
Manager and Spurs former players team regular

name: Peter Crouch
honour: Goal that sealed Spurs’ first Champions League place
line: The header that took Spurs into the Champions League, and a second career as one of football’s funniest storytellers.
bio: Peter Crouch joined Spurs from Portsmouth in 2009, reuniting with Harry Redknapp. In May 2010 he headed the winner at Manchester City that secured fourth place and Champions League football for the first time.

In that first European campaign he scored a hat-trick against Young Boys in the qualifying round and the goal that won the last-16 first leg against AC Milan at San Siro, as Spurs reached the quarter-finals. He moved on to Stoke City in 2011.
Since retiring he has built a hugely popular media career across television, podcasting and books, with a self-deprecating style that makes him one of the most natural hosts in the game.
why: Best for audiences who want laughter with substance: conferences, awards nights, client dinners and internal comms moments that need warmth.
timeline: Header at Man City seals Champions League qualification
Hat-trick against Young Boys in the play-off
Winner against AC Milan at San Siro; joins Stoke City

name: Michael Dawson
line: Nine years of total commitment at the back. A grounded voice on leadership, consistency and putting the team first.
bio: Michael Dawson joined Spurs from Nottingham Forest in 2005 and quickly became a dressing-room leader: a no-nonsense centre-back who threw himself in front of everything and never hid on a bad day.

He started the 2008 League Cup final win over Chelsea, was part of the Redknapp side that reached the Champions League, and was called into England's squad for the 2010 World Cup. He later captained the club before moving on to Hull City in 2014.
Fans still sing his name, and he remains a familiar face for the Spurs former players team and in the media, talking with honesty and humour about the game.
why: Best for leadership and team-development audiences who value reliability, effort and leading by example.
timeline: Joins Tottenham Hotspur from Nottingham Forest
Starts the League Cup final win at Wembley
Called into England’s World Cup squad
Joins Hull City after nine years in N17
Spurs former players team regular and media work

name: Benoît Assou-Ekotto
line: The cult-hero left-back who always said exactly what he thought. Refreshing, funny and unlike any other footballer you will meet.
bio: Benoît Assou-Ekotto joined Spurs from Lens in 2006 and became one of the most distinctive figures of the Redknapp era: a calm, attacking left-back with a trademark hairstyle and the occasional thunderous long-range strike.

He represented Cameroon at the 2010 and 2014 World Cups. Off the pitch he became famous for refreshingly frank interviews about life as a professional footballer, which made him a genuine cult hero with supporters.
He still turns out for the Spurs former players team, and his straight-talking perspective on work, identity and doing things your own way lands with audiences well beyond football.
why: Best for audiences who want authenticity: culture and inclusion sessions, creative teams and events that reward a different point of view.
timeline: Plays at the World Cup for Cameroon
First-choice left-back in the Redknapp side

name: Rafael van der Vaart
line: The deadline-day signing who lit up White Hart Lane. Craft, confidence and a big-game temperament from a World Cup finalist.
bio: Rafael van der Vaart arrived from Real Madrid on transfer deadline day in 2010, weeks after playing in the World Cup final for the Netherlands, and immediately became the creative heartbeat of Harry Redknapp's side.

Clever, combative and decisive, he scored regularly from midfield and loved the north London derby, including a role in the comeback win at the Emirates in November 2010. He returned to Hamburg in 2012 and later played in Spain and Denmark.
Since retiring he has become a well-known football analyst on Dutch television, and he remains a hugely popular figure whenever he returns to N17.
why: Best for audiences who want flair with conviction: client hospitality, international teams and creative or product leaders.
timeline: Plays in the World Cup final with the Netherlands
Joins Spurs from Real Madrid on deadline day
Part of the comeback derby win at the Emirates

name: Mousa Dembélé
line: The quiet genius at the centre of Pochettino’s Spurs. Balance, calm and the art of making the hard things look simple.
bio: Mousa Dembélé joined Spurs from Fulham in 2012 and became one of the most admired midfielders of his generation: almost impossible to dispossess, physically powerful and remarkably calm with the ball at his feet.

He was central to the Pochettino side that challenged for the title, finishing second in 2016–17, and teammates and opponents alike spoke of him with something close to awe. With Belgium he won a bronze medal at the 2018 World Cup.
He left for China in January 2019 and has since retired. He is famously private and understated, which gives his reflections on composure and teamwork real weight.
why: Best for smaller, high-trust rooms: leadership dinners, coaching cohorts and teams who value composure over noise.
timeline: Part of the side that challenges for the title

name: Aaron Lennon
line: A decade of blistering pace down the right. A grounded, generous voice on speed, longevity and looking after yourself.
bio: Aaron Lennon joined Spurs from Leeds United as a teenager in 2005 and spent a decade terrorising full-backs with his pace and directness on the right wing.
He started the 2008 League Cup final win over Chelsea and was a key outlet in the Redknapp side that reached the Champions League. With England he went to both the 2006 and 2010 World Cups.
After leaving for Everton in 2015 he played on at Burnley and abroad. Today he is a regular for the Spurs former players team, where the crowd's reaction shows how fondly he is remembered.
why: Best for audiences who want a down-to-earth story about speed, longevity and staying yourself through the highs and lows.
timeline: Joins Tottenham Hotspur from Leeds United
Goes to the World Cup with England
Starts the League Cup final win at Wembley
Joins Everton after a decade at Spurs

name: Paul Robinson
line: England’s number one and a Wembley winner with Spurs. Straight talk on pressure, mistakes and the loneliest position on the pitch.
bio: Paul Robinson joined Spurs from Leeds United in 2004 and was the club's first-choice goalkeeper through the Martin Jol years, when White Hart Lane got used to European nights again.

He was England's number one at the 2006 World Cup, kept goal in the 2008 League Cup final win over Chelsea, and even scored for Spurs, with a huge free-kick from his own half that bounced over the Watford goalkeeper in 2007.
He later played for Blackburn Rovers and Burnley. Goalkeeping teaches you to live with public mistakes and move on fast, and he talks about that with refreshing candour.
why: Best for audiences dealing with pressure and accountability: finance, operations and leadership teams where one error is very visible.
timeline: Joins Tottenham Hotspur from Leeds United
England’s number one at the World Cup
Scores from his own half against Watford
Wins the League Cup at Wembley; joins Blackburn Rovers

name: Ossie Ardiles
honour: World Cup winner 1978 · FA Cup winner 1981
line: The World Cup winner who swapped Buenos Aires for N17 and became part of the club's soul. A story of courage, craft and making a new home.
bio: Ossie Ardiles arrived at White Hart Lane in the summer of 1978, weeks after winning the World Cup with Argentina. Signing two world champions alongside Ricky Villa was one of the boldest moves in English football at the time, and Ardiles quickly won the crowd over with his quick feet, intelligence and appetite for the game.

He was at the heart of the side that won the FA Cup in 1981, a final that gave the club and its supporters a song still sung today, and he was part of the squad that went on to European success in 1984. Few overseas players have meant as much to a club's identity.

He returned as manager in 1993 with a fearless, attack-first approach, and has remained close to the club ever since, including work as a Tottenham Hotspur ambassador and managing the Spurs former players team sides. He brings warmth, humour and a unique perspective on moving countries and leading with conviction.
why: Best for audiences who want a global story: international teams, leadership events and client dinners that celebrate courage and culture.
timeline: Wins the World Cup with Argentina, then joins Tottenham Hotspur
Moves on after a decade at the club
Club ambassador and the Spurs former players team manager

name: Martin Jol
honour: Back-to-back fifth-place finishes and a UEFA Cup quarter-final
line: The big Dutchman who restored belief at White Hart Lane, built a young, attacking side and brought European nights back to N17.
bio: Martin Jol came to Spurs in 2004 as part of a new coaching team and was handed the top job within months. A former Netherlands international who had played in England, he understood the league and quickly connected with supporters through his honesty and presence on the touchline.

He built an energetic, attacking team around young players who would become Spurs favourites, finishing fifth in consecutive Premier League seasons and taking the club back into Europe, where it reached the UEFA Cup quarter-finals in 2007.

After leaving in 2007 he managed at the top level in Germany, the Netherlands and England. His talks focus on rebuilding a team's confidence, backing young talent and keeping a dressing room together under scrutiny.
why: Best for leadership audiences focused on rebuilding confidence, developing young talent and leading in the public eye.
timeline: Joins the Spurs coaching staff and is appointed head coach
Second fifth-place finish; UEFA Cup quarter-final

name: Chris Hughton
pos: Full-back 1979–1990 · Spurs coach 1993–2007 · Republic of Ireland
honour: FA Cup winner 1981 & 1982 · UEFA Cup winner 1984
line: Academy product, cup winner and then the coach who served Spurs for well over a decade. Leadership with calm, integrity and a lot of quiet strength.
bio: Chris Hughton came through the Spurs youth system and became a dependable, attacking full-back in one of the club's most successful sides, winning the FA Cup in 1981 and 1982 and the UEFA Cup in 1984. At international level he represented the Republic of Ireland.

After his playing days he returned to Spurs as a coach and stayed for well over a decade, working with the reserves and the first team and serving a long line of managers. Few people have seen the inside of the club from so many angles.

He went on to manage at the highest level, winning promotion to the Premier League more than once and later leading a national team. He is widely respected for his composure and integrity, and speaks thoughtfully on leadership, inclusion and building trust.
why: Best for audiences who value calm, principled leadership: management development, inclusion programmes and coaching cultures.
timeline: First-team debut after coming through the youth system
Returns to Spurs as a coach
Leaves the coaching staff to begin a management career

name: Steffen Freund
honour: League Cup winner 1999 · European champion with Germany
line: The German terrier the Lane adored, who came back as assistant head coach. Energy, standards and an insider view of elite coaching.
bio: Steffen Freund arrived from Borussia Dortmund at the end of 1998 already a European champion with Germany and an established player at one of Europe's leading clubs. At White Hart Lane he became a cult hero for his relentless running, tackling and visible passion, and he was part of the side that won the League Cup at Wembley in 1999.

He returned to the club in 2012 as assistant head coach, working on the training ground and touchline with the first team, so he has experienced Spurs both as a player and from inside the coaching staff.

Today he is a familiar face in the Spurs former players team line-ups and in football broadcasting. He speaks with energy and humour about work rate, adapting to a new culture and the detail behind elite coaching.
why: Best for audiences who want energy and standards: sales kick-offs, team away-days and coaching-focused sessions.
timeline: Wins the European Championship with Germany
Joins Tottenham Hotspur from Borussia Dortmund

name: Steve Perryman
honour: Spurs' record appearance maker · FA Cup-winning captain
line: No one has played more games for Spurs. The captain who lifted the FA Cup twice and the definitive voice on loyalty and leadership.
bio: Steve Perryman joined Spurs as a teenager and made his first-team debut in 1969. Over the next seventeen years he played more games for the club than anyone in its history, first as a tireless midfielder and later as a defender.

He won the League Cup and the UEFA Cup in the early 1970s, then captained the side that lifted the FA Cup in 1981 and 1982. In 1982 the Football Writers' Association named him Footballer of the Year, and he won his England cap that same year.

He later returned to Spurs as assistant manager, briefly taking charge as caretaker, and built a long coaching career that included years in Japanese football. He speaks with authority on captaincy, consistency and what loyalty really looks like over a career.
why: Best for audiences exploring leadership and longevity: leadership programmes, long-service awards and club partner dinners.
timeline: Captains Spurs to back-to-back FA Cups

name: Ricky Villa
honour: Scored the winner in the 1981 FA Cup final replay
line: Scorer of the most famous goal in Spurs history. A story about bouncing back from a bad day on the biggest stage.
bio: Ricky Villa joined Spurs from Argentina in 1978 alongside Ossie Ardiles, part of the World Cup-winning squad and one of the first overseas stars of the modern English game.

His defining moment came in 1981. Substituted in the first FA Cup final against Manchester City, he was given another chance in the replay and scored twice, including a dribbling solo winner that is still regarded as one of the greatest goals ever scored at Wembley.

After leaving Spurs he played and coached in the Americas, and he remains a beloved figure in N17 whenever he returns. His story is a natural fit for any audience thinking about setbacks, second chances and seizing the moment.
why: Best for audiences who need a bounce-back story: sales teams after a tough quarter, resilience programmes and celebratory dinners.
timeline: Joins Tottenham Hotspur from Argentina with Ossie Ardiles
Substituted in the FA Cup final, then scores twice in the replay to win it
Leaves for a new chapter in the Americas
Returns to N17 as a celebrated guest

name: David Ginola
honour: PFA and FWA Player of the Year 1999
line: Flair, style and the 1999 double of player awards. The Lane's great entertainer on confidence, creativity and owning the stage.
bio: David Ginola joined Spurs from Newcastle in the summer of 1997 and became one of the most thrilling players ever to grace White Hart Lane, a winger who could beat defenders for fun and lift a crowd with a single run.

His 1998–99 season was exceptional. He helped Spurs win the League Cup at Wembley and was named Player of the Year by both his fellow professionals and the football writers, a rare double for a player outside the title-winning sides.

Since retiring he has worked across broadcasting, fashion and brand campaigns, and he remains a natural on stage. He talks with charm about confidence, creativity and expressing yourself under pressure.
why: Best for brand launches, creative industries and client events that want star quality and a touch of French flair.
timeline: Joins Tottenham Hotspur from Newcastle United
PFA Players’ Player and FWA Footballer of the Year

name: Jenna Schillaci
honour: Captained Spurs into the Women’s Super League
line: The long-serving captain who led Spurs Women up the pyramid and into the WSL. Now one of the game's familiar broadcasting voices.
bio: Jenna Schillaci spent many seasons at Tottenham Hotspur and became the captain of a side that climbed the women's football pyramid step by step, at a time when the women's game was still fighting for resources and recognition.
That journey culminated in promotion to the Women's Super League in 2019, and she led the team into its first top-flight season, helping lay the foundations the club has built on since.

Since hanging up her boots she has become a familiar face presenting and analysing women's football on television. She speaks with clarity about leadership in a growing organisation, perseverance and the changing landscape of the women's game.
why: Best for audiences championing growth and inclusion: women's networks, scale-up teams and International Women's Day events.
timeline: Becomes a mainstay and then captain of Tottenham Hotspur Ladies
Promotion to the Women’s Super League
Captains Spurs in their first WSL season

name: Kerys Harrop
pos: Defender · Tottenham Hotspur Women · WSL Hall of Fame
line: A WSL original and Hall of Famer who brought top-flight know-how to Spurs' first years in the league. Consistency, leadership and doing the basics brilliantly.
bio: Kerys Harrop was one of the original players of the Women's Super League, establishing herself as a dependable defender at Birmingham City from the league's first season.

She joined Tottenham Hotspur in 2019 as the club stepped up to the top flight, bringing experience and organisation to a young squad and becoming a leader in the dressing room during Spurs' first years in the WSL.

In 2026 she was inducted into the Barclays WSL Hall of Fame in recognition of her contribution to the league. She speaks about consistency, professionalism through a period of rapid change, and leading by example.
why: Best for audiences who value steady leadership: women's networks, team-building days and organisations going through growth.
timeline: Plays in the first Women’s Super League season
Joins Tottenham Hotspur as the club enters the WSL
Part of Spurs’ first WSL campaign
Inducted into the Barclays WSL Hall of Fame

name: Micky van de Ven
line: The club captain with a sprinter's engine. A Dutch centre-back who leads from the front and talks about standards, speed and taking responsibility.
bio: Micky van de Ven arrived from Wolfsburg in 2023 and quickly became one of the most recognisable defenders in the Premier League, known for recovery pace that turns last-ditch moments into routine ones.
He was part of the side that won the 2025 Europa League final in Bilbao, and in August 2026 he was named club captain at the head of a five-man leadership group.
why: Best for leadership audiences and client events that want the current captain: standards, accountability and leading a dressing room in public.
timeline: Joins Tottenham Hotspur from VfL Wolfsburg
Wins the Europa League in Bilbao

name: Pedro Porro
line: A world champion in N17. The attacking full-back who came home from the 2026 World Cup with a winners' medal and the energy to match.
bio: Pedro Porro joined from Sporting CP in 2023 and made the right flank his own: an attacking full-back who loves to drive forward and deliver from wide.

He won the Europa League with Spurs in 2025 and the following summer joined the club's short list of World Cup winners as part of Spain's 2026 squad. He is one of the five players in the 2026–27 leadership group.
why: Best for audiences who want a winner's story told with warmth: sales kick-offs, Spanish-speaking teams and partner events.
timeline: Joins Tottenham Hotspur from Sporting CP
Wins the Europa League with Spurs
Wins the FIFA World Cup with Spain
Named in the club's leadership group

name: James Maddison
line: The No. 10 with the personality to match the shirt. Creative, funny and candid about confidence, comebacks and carrying a dressing room.
bio: James Maddison came through Coventry City's academy, made his name at Norwich and Leicester, and joined Spurs in 2023 as the side's creative heartbeat.
An England international and one of the club's five captains for 2026–27, he is one of the most natural communicators in the squad, on and off the pitch.
why: Best for audiences who want personality: brand content, fan events and teams that need a lift.
timeline: Joins Tottenham Hotspur from Leicester City

name: Ben Davies
line: The squad's longest-serving player. More than a decade in Lilywhite, a Wales stalwart, and the steady voice every dressing room needs.
bio: Ben Davies signed from his boyhood club Swansea City in 2014 and has been part of every chapter since, from White Hart Lane to the new stadium, across several head coaches and generations of team-mates.
A long-serving Wales international, he reached the semi-finals of Euro 2016 with his country. He remains part of the club's leadership group for 2026–27.
why: Best for audiences interested in loyalty, consistency and being the dependable one: long-service awards, leadership programmes and partner events.

name: Archie Gray
short: Midfielder · Europa League winner · England U21
line: A young leader already. Europa League winner, European Under-21 champion and part of the leadership group before his 21st birthday.
bio: Archie Gray joined from Leeds United in 2024 and adapted quickly, playing in midfield and across the back line as the team needed.

He won the Europa League with Spurs and the European Under-21 Championship with England in 2025, was recognised by supporters in the 2025–26 Player of the Season awards, and was named in the club's leadership group for 2026–27.
why: Best for early-careers and graduate audiences: versatility, maturity beyond your years and stepping up early.

name: Dominic Solanke
line: The centre-forward who leads the line. An England striker with a story about persistence, from academy prodigy to the man who carries the attack.
bio: Dominic Solanke joined from AFC Bournemouth in August 2024 and became the focal point of the attack, a striker who works as hard for the team as he does in the box.
He started the 2025 Europa League final win in Bilbao. Earlier in his career he won the Under-20 World Cup with England in 2017, and he has represented England at senior level.
why: Best for audiences interested in persistence and patience: teams in a rebuilding phase, sales audiences and youth programmes.

name: Richarlison
line: All heart and plenty of fire. A Brazil forward and Olympic champion who brings energy, emotion and a genuine connection with fans.
bio: Richarlison joined from Everton in 2022, bringing the passion and work rate that have made him a fan favourite wherever he has played.

He won Olympic gold with Brazil at Tokyo 2020, played at the 2022 World Cup and started the 2025 Europa League final win. Off the pitch he is one of the squad's most natural connectors with supporters.
why: Best for fan-facing and brand work that needs energy: activations, community events and Portuguese-speaking audiences.

name: Andy Robertson
line: Scotland's captain, now in Lilywhite. A left-back whose rise from Scottish amateur football to the top of the game is a masterclass in hunger.
bio: Andy Robertson joined Spurs in the summer of 2026 after nine years at Liverpool, where he won the Premier League twice and became one of the best-known full-backs in Europe.
Captain of Scotland, he worked his way up from Queen's Park through Dundee United and Hull City, a route that gives him a rare perspective on rejection, graft and making the most of a chance.
why: Best for audiences who want a hunger-and-graft story: sales teams, career-changers and leadership events.
talks: Making the most of a chance

name: Xavi Simons
line: A playmaker raised in two of football's great academies. Flair, fearlessness and a global following.
bio: Xavi Simons developed at Barcelona's La Masia and Paris Saint-Germain before starring in Eindhoven and Leipzig, then joined Spurs in August 2025.
A Netherlands international who reached the semi-finals of Euro 2024, he is one of the most creative players in the squad, with a big social following and a natural feel for content.
why: Best for brand and content work aimed at younger, international audiences.
timeline: Joins Tottenham Hotspur from RB Leipzig

name: Mohammed Kudus
line: Close control, big moments and a huge following across Africa. A Ghana international who plays with joy.
bio: Mohammed Kudus joined from West Ham United in July 2025, bringing dribbling, power and an eye for the spectacular to the attack.

A Ghana international who previously played for Ajax, he is one of the most popular African players in the Premier League, with strong appeal for partners targeting audiences in West Africa and the diaspora.

name: Destiny Udogie
line: Power, pace and a big smile. The Italy full-back who bombs forward and brings warmth to any room.
bio: Destiny Udogie signed from Udinese in 2022, spent a season back in Italy on loan and arrived in north London for 2023–24, quickly becoming a fixture at left-back.
An Italy international, he started the 2025 Europa League final win in Bilbao.

name: Lucas Bergvall
line: A Swedish midfielder who arrived as a teenager and grew up in the Premier League spotlight.
bio: Lucas Bergvall joined from Djurgården in 2024 and made an immediate impression in his first season, earning a regular place in midfield while still a teenager.
A Sweden international, he brings composure on the ball and a calm, thoughtful voice that suits early-careers and youth audiences.
why: Best for graduate, early-careers and youth audiences, and Scandinavian partners.

name: Rodrigo Bentancur
line: The experienced midfielder who keeps the team ticking. Boca-raised, Juventus-schooled, Uruguay through and through.
bio: Rodrigo Bentancur came through at Boca Juniors, spent five seasons at Juventus and joined Spurs in January 2022.
A Uruguay international and a calm presence in midfield, he started the 2025 Europa League final win.

name: Conor Gallagher
line: Relentless in midfield. An England international from just down the road who brings energy and work rate to every minute.
bio: Conor Gallagher came through Chelsea's academy, made his name on loan around the Football League and in the Premier League, and spent time with Atlético Madrid before joining Spurs in January 2026.
An England international who was part of the Euro 2024 squad, he is known for a high-energy, all-action style that makes him an easy fit for audiences who value effort.
why: Best for audiences who value work rate: sales teams, kick-offs and grassroots or community programmes.

name: Sandro Tonali
honour: Serie A winner with AC Milan
line: The Italy midfielder with the quarterback's range of passing. A 2026 signing with a title already on his CV.
bio: Sandro Tonali came through at Brescia, won Serie A with AC Milan and moved to Newcastle United before joining Spurs in July 2026.
An Italy international, he controls games from deep with range of passing and tireless running.

name: Mathys Tel
line: A young French forward with speed, skill and a big future. Rennes academy, Bayern Munich, now N17.
bio: Mathys Tel came through the Rennes academy, moved to Bayern Munich as a teenager and joined Spurs on loan in February 2025 before the move became permanent that summer.
Quick and direct, he is one of the younger forwards in the squad and a natural fit for youth and grassroots audiences.
why: Best for youth, schools and grassroots audiences, and French-speaking partners.

name: Drew Spence
line: The captain at the heart of Spurs Women. Experience, calm and a career that spans the whole modern history of the WSL.
bio: Drew Spence spent well over a decade at Chelsea before joining Spurs in 2022, bringing experience from the earliest days of the Women's Super League.
A Jamaica international who helped her country qualify for the 2023 Women's World Cup, she was named Spurs Women captain for 2026–27.
why: Best for women's sport, inclusion and leadership audiences, and partner events celebrating the growth of the women's game.

name: Eveliina Summanen
honour: Spurs Women's all-time WSL assist leader
line: The creator-in-chief. A Finland international who has set up more WSL goals than anyone in Spurs Women's history.
bio: Eveliina Summanen joined Spurs in January 2022 and has become one of the most important players in the club's Women's Super League story.
A Finland international, she has provided more WSL assists than any other Spurs player, a record built on vision, set-piece delivery and consistency.
why: Best for audiences interested in teamwork and making others better: collaboration workshops, Nordic partners and women's sport events.

name: Jessica Naz
line: One of our own. Joined the club at 12, grew up with the women's team and wrote herself into its history as a centurion.
bio: Jessica Naz joined Spurs as a 12-year-old and has been part of the women's team through its rise into the Women's Super League.
In April 2024 she became a Spurs centurion. Her path from academy to first team makes her a natural fit for grassroots, schools and community audiences.
